title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization

paper.title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
paper.abstract: Abstract Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO) . For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step’s baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory’s eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

CCPO combines contextually weighted peer comparisons and short-horizon future progress for critic-free step-level credit assignment. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks through sustained environment interaction ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Benchmarks such as WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024a ) and SWE-bench ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) require information gathering, coordinated actions, and adaptation to feedback. Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) provides a post-training framework that optimizes policies using rewards from interaction trajectories. Recent applications span open-web research, web navigation, and multi-step software engineering ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Qi et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . However, feedback often arrives only after many decisions. Learning from such delayed feedback depends on how it is translated into policy updates. PPO-based actor–critic methods use learned value estimates to guide optimization, at the cost of training an additional value model ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Alternatively, group-based methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) estimate relative advantages from multiple sampled outcomes without a separately learned value critic. When applied at the trajectory level, however, a single advantage is shared across all actions in a rollout. Such comparisons differentiate outcomes across trajectories but provide limited information about the contributions of individual decisions, especially when rewards are sparse and delayed ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . To enable fine-grained policy updates, recent methods extend this approach to construct step-level advantage estimates: GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) compares actions encountered at shared observations, and G2PO ( Wang et al., 2026d ) incorporates the structure of transitions between observation groups. HGPO ( He et al., 2026 ) accounts for historical context by organizing comparisons into hierarchical groups. In each case, step-level credit comes from comparing experiences in existing rollouts, so it depends on how they are compared. Two challenges remain when steps are compared at matched observations. The first is whom a step should be compared with. Identical observations can occur after different preceding actions, reasoning, exploration depth, and accumulated contexts. Peers that share an observation are therefore not equally informative for the step being evaluated (the query). Requiring peers to share the same history instead leaves few peers per step, and a baseline averaged over so few returns gives noisy advantages ( He et al., 2026 ) . Our premise is that, within observation-matched groups, contextual similarity should determine each peer’s contribution to the query’s baseline and value estimates. The second is what a step should be credited for. A return comparison credits a step for belonging to a trajectory that ended well, but an eventual success can include redundant actions or detours. Separating a step that inherits a favorable context from one that makes progress from it requires a complementary comparison of realized gains over a short continuation. To address both challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO) . For the first, CCPO represents each step’s context with semantic features of an interaction window from a frozen LLM and accumulated trajectory statistics, and gives greater weight to observation-matched peers with higher contextual similarity (Figure 1 ). For the second, CCPO builds two credit signals on these weighted peers. Historical credit compares the realized return with its contextual peer baseline. Future credit measures short-horizon progress as the change in contextual value, a weighted average of peers’ discounted terminal rewards, between the current step and a later step of the same rollout. Both are computed in hindsight from collected rollouts without requiring an auxiliary value critic or additional environment interactions. On agentic multi-step benchmarks, ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) and WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , CCPO outperforms prompting- and RL-based baselines using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbones ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) . Our main contributions are as follows: • Contextual credit estimation from history and future progress. We assign step-level credit by combining a history-conditioned return residual with estimated value change over a future horizon, capturing outcome-relative performance and local progress. Analysis shows complementary effects of history and future credit as learning evolves. • Contextual similarity for step-level peer weighting. We aggregate peer returns with continuous weights set by the similarity between query and peer context representations, producing a context-dependent baseline. Replacing these weights with uniform ones lowers success by 3.7 and 2.6 points. • Semantic and structural context representations. We combine semantic hidden states of recent interactions with accumulated trajectory statistics, enabling context-sensitive comparisons across trajectories without training an auxiliary value critic. 2 Related Work Agentic reinforcement learning for long-horizon tasks. Reinforcement learning (RL) ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve through extended interactions in which observations, reasoning, actions, and feedback accumulate into trajectories ( Zhou et al., 2024b ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Applications span interactive gaming, web navigation, open-web research, and multi-step software engineering ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026b ; Luo et al., 2025 ) , where agents act in an environment and adapt to its feedback over many steps. Another line of work trains agents to reason with external tools, including search engines, web browsing tools, and code interpreters ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Tongyi DeepResearch Team and others, 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . Agentic RL can also learn from successes and failures through verbal reflection and trajectory preference learning ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Putta et al., 2024 ) . To collect high-quality trajectories, methods use uncertainty-guided branching and resampling ( Dong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Reward design ( Wang et al., 2026e ) is also crucial, spanning outcome-supervised reward models ( Qi et al., 2025 ) , process rewards from environment-aware models such as DataPRM ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) , and turn-level reward assignment ( Tao et al., 2026 ) . Despite these advances, sparse and delayed rewards, costly environment interaction, and training instability remain challenges ( Tao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) , motivating efficient and stable policy optimization from trajectories already collected. Policy optimization for LLM agents. Existing approaches differ in their optimization objectives and advantage estimators. Preference-based methods, including DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , ETO ( Song et al., 2024 ) , and Agent Q ( Putta et al., 2024 ) , optimize policies from response or trajectory preferences, including successful and failed agent rollouts, without explicit reward-model fitting. Actor–critic methods use learned value estimates, as in PPO-based reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with InstructGPT ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and multi-step agent learning with ArCHer ( Zhou et al., 2024b ) . To avoid a separate value critic, group-based methods estimate advantages from multiple sampled responses or trajectories. RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) uses the mean reward of other samples as a baseline, while GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , used in DeepSeek-R1 ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , standardizes group rewards. Related variants include LOOP ( Chen et al., 2025 ) with leave-one-out PPO updates and Dr. GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) with revised length and reward normalization. Further refinements target update stability and exploration efficiency through clipping, importance weighting, and sampling, including DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025a ) , CISPO ( MiniMax and others, 2025 ) , SAPO ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , VESPO ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , SAMPO ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , Clip-Cov ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , and T 2 PO ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . However, trajectory-level applications of outcome-supervised GRPO share a single advantage across all actions in a rollout, without explicitly differentiating individual contributions ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . This motivates the step-level methods discussed next. Step-level credit assignment. Recent methods construct step-level learning signals for multi-step interactions ( Zhang, 2026 ) . Critic-based methods include SWEET-RL ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) with additional training-time information and HCAPO ( Tan et al., 2026 ) with the agent as a hindsight critic. TRACE ( Tao et al., 2026 ) derives turn-level rewards from a frozen model’s gold-answer likelihoods. OpenClaw-RL ( Wang et al., 2026c ) combines evaluative rewards and corrective hints extracted from next-state feedback. Other methods estimate advantages by comparing collected trajectories. GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) combines episode-level advantages with comparisons at matching observations, while HGPO ( He et al., 2026 ) aggregates advantages from hierarchical groups matched at different history lengths. SALT ( Li et al., 2026a ) constructs graphs from trajectories of the same prompt, while G2PO ( Wang et al., 2026d ) aggregates observations into a state-transition graph to estimate values and advantages. GEPO ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) uses task-conditioned graph centrality to shape trajectory returns and scale step-level advantages. Peer matching faces a granularity trade-off: observation-only matching can mix different histories, whereas exact history matching reduces the available samples ( He et al., 2026 ) . CCPO keeps all observation-matched peers and weights each by the similarity of its context to the query’s, characterized by local semantic and accumulated trajectory features, thus enabling fine-grained comparisons utilizing available peers. 3 Contextual Credit Policy Optimization Figure 2 : Contextual credit policy optimization of multi-step tasks. See Appendix C for details. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate CCPO against baseline methods on ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) and WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , covering household task execution and online shopping through multi-step interaction. ALFWorld comprises six household task categories, with 3,553 training tasks and 140 held-out tasks of the in-distribution evaluation split. For WebShop, we follow the goal partition implemented in verl-agent ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , reserving the first 500 goals as the evaluation pool and sampling training tasks from the remaining goals. Following prior work ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026d ) , we report overall and per-category success rates on ALFWorld. For WebShop, we report success rate and mean task score. Models and baselines. We use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) as policy backbones. We compare CCPO with three categories of baselines: (1) Off-the-shelf LLMs: Gemini 3.8 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) , DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI and others, 2026 ) , and Qwen3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) . (2) Prompt-based agents: the Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones without task-specific RL fine-tuning, ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , and Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . (3) RL training methods: PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , HGPO ( He et al., 2026 ) , and G2PO ( Wang et al., 2026d ) . Baseline configurations are detailed in Appendix B . Implementation details. We train CCPO using verl-agent ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , built on veRL ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) , for 150 iterations, sampling 16 tasks with eight trajectories each per iteration. We use a learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} and discount factor 0.95. Interaction limits are 50 steps for ALFWorld and 15 for WebShop. Settings are shared across both backbones and all group-based baselines, except that HGPO retains its published limits of 4,096 prompt tokens on ALFWorld and 30 interaction steps on WebShop. CCPO uses a K H = 2 K_{H}=2 history window and a K F = 2 K_{F}=2 future horizon. We evaluate two CCPO variants, a default and an episode-augmented one. The default uses A CC A_{\mathrm{CC}} from Equation ( 8 ). The variant uses A CC + A EP A_{\mathrm{CC}}+A_{\mathrm{EP}} , adding a standard episode-level advantage without further normalization. All training and evaluation are completed on 8 × \times H200 GPUs. We report means and standard deviations across three random seeds. Appendix B gives the shared training budgets and optimization settings. Appendix D provides an ALFWorld prompt and response example. 4.2 Main Results Comparison with baselines. CCPO weights observation-matched peers by contextual similarity and pairs historical credit with future credit, both computed from collected rollouts without an auxiliary value critic. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, it reaches 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop. In ablations, uniform weights lower success by 3.7 and 2.6 points, and either credit alone lowers it by up to 12.3. Limitations. CCPO has three main limitations. First, our evaluation covers two multi-step benchmarks and one model family. Broader generalization and applicability to short-horizon or single-step tasks remain untested. Second, exact observation matching can limit peer availability, while fixed temporal windows and hand-designed trajectory statistics may require adaptation across environments. Finally, future credit vanishes when all rollouts in a task group receive zero terminal reward, limiting the future channel’s contribution under sparse rewards, particularly early in training when successful trajectories are scarce. Future work. The changing balance between historical and future credit motivates adaptive horizons and stage-dependent weighting. Further directions include streaming credit estimation from incomplete rollouts, multimodal contexts combining visual observations and textual histories, semantic peer retrieval beyond exact observation matching, and uncertainty estimates for correlated visits. Broader evaluation should examine generalization across model families and domains, computational scaling, and the effects of realized-future conditioning on policy updates.
